kernelIdea: {x | p(x)} is the set of all x making p(x) true — a set defined by a condition rather than a list.

kernels.l1: You can make a box by naming a rule instead of putting things in one at a time.
kernels.l2: There are two ways to make a box: list what goes in it, or give a rule that decides. The same box can be made both ways.
kernels.l3: You can describe a set by listing its elements, or by giving a condition: {x | x is a whole number between 0 and 5} means "the set of all x such that…". The condition does the choosing for you.
kernels.l4: {x ∈ A | p(x)} denotes the set of elements of A that satisfy p. A condition replaces a list, which is the only way to describe sets too large to write down.
kernels.l5: Set-builder notation {x ∈ A | p(x)} turns an open statement into a set; this is where Chapter 1's predicates become Chapter 2's objects.
kernels.l6: A set may be specified by an extensional list or by an intensional condition on a stated ambient set; the ambient set is not optional.
kernels.l7: Set-builder notation {x ∈ A | p(x)} converts a predicate into a set by separation from an existing set A. The condition is a statement in the sense of Chapter 1, which is where Chapter 1 becomes a tool.
kernels.l8: Set-builder is the Axiom Schema of Separation in notation; unrestricted comprehension {x | p(x)} is inconsistent, which is why the ambient set may not be dropped.
